mn108:2.1: ‘Fortified’ (paṭisaṅkhārāpeti) is a word not found in the P.T.S. Dictionary.
mn108:5.4: This means that there was no Arahant who equalled the Buddha in all knowledges and powers, though all had equally exhausted the taints and realized Nibbāna.
mn108:6.8: The Buddha is frequently referred to as ‘Arahant’, as here; the elevation of the Buddha to a super-Enlightened figure is the work of later writers—especially in the Mahāyāna—who have tried, in the wrong way, to praise the Buddha. He is rightly praised not by worldly aggrandizement but by pure practice and realization.
mn108:7.4: This reply is of interest in view of the later Buddhist schools’ claims to various ‘patriarchal’ successions, sometimes including the venerable Ānanda himself.
mn108:10.17: According to the classification of offences in the Pātimokkha and elsewhere in the Vinaya. See ‘The Pātimokkha Rule’, Mahamakut Press, Bangkok.
mn108:15.2: That is, by repetition of them.
mn108:26.4: The Commentary explains ‘making it the main thing’ (antaraṁ karitvā) as making it the main cause of his meditating, since it is by the power of sensual lust that this ‘meditating’ comes about. These four terms—meditates on it, about it, because of it, over it—are chosen to show how useless are the efforts of a ‘meditator’ who puts the five hindrances first in his life. Cf. Sutta 113.
mn108:26.13: This, of course, is not jhāna in the true sense of the word.
